source.version: Published journal article: Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 2023, 39(5), 40-58; DOI 10.14742/ajet.8923 (PDF pp. 1 and 19, journal header and recommended citation).
source.title_on_document: Effects of a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach on learners’ courseware project performances and perceptions

supplement.holds: No appendix or supplementary material is referenced in the complete PDF. The rubric and all reported quantitative outcome tables are in the main article (PDF pp. 10-13, Tables 1-8); references occupy PDF pp. 15-19.

paper_design_summary: Students in two intact university classes learned to design multimedia courseware using PowerPoint; one class was randomly assigned to ChatGPT-based flipped learning through Tencent QQ, and the other received conventional flipped learning (PDF p. 9, Participants and Experimental procedure). Instructors scored pre- and post-project quality, while questionnaires measured creative-thinking tendency, self-efficacy, learning attitudes and motivation (PDF pp. 10-13, Data collection instruments and Tables 1-8). The paper calls the design quasi-experimental, but explicitly reports class-level random allocation; neither the exact scored project prompt nor AI access during the post-project assessment is specified.

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of two intact classes was randomly assigned to ChatGPT-FLGA; the other class received T-FLGA. This is class-level allocation within ordinary coursework, not individual student randomization. The author labels the study quasi-experimental; the randomization method is not described (PDF pp. 1 and 9).
assignment.quote: One of two classes was randomly assigned to the experimental group, while the other was assigned to the control group.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 40), abstract; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Participants.

arms.name: ChatGPT-FLGA
arms.description: Experimental intact class: ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach, including an AI teacher accessed through Tencent QQ, personalized dialogue, assignment reminders and learning-participation feedback. Both classes received flipped instruction and QQ discussions with the same teacher (PDF pp. 1, 5-9).

arms.name: T-FLGA
arms.description: Control intact class: traditional flipped learning guiding approach with instructional resources and QQ discussions, taught by the same teacher, without the ChatGPT-FLGA system (PDF pp. 1 and 9; PDF p. 13, Discussion).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The class sizes given at allocation are retained in every outcome table: 42 experimental and 39 control (PDF p. 9, Participants; PDF pp. 11-13, Tables 2-8). Counts under n_randomized denote students in the allocated classes, not independently randomized individuals.
participants.who: Chemistry majors taking the compulsory Modern Educational Technology course at a public normal university; average age 20, with no prior knowledge of designing and developing courseware (PDF p. 9, Participants; PDF p. 15, Limitations and future research).
participants.quote: A total of 81 participants (aged 20 on average) were from two classes
participants.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Participants and Experimental procedure; PDF pp. 11-13 (printed pp. 50-52), Tables 2-8; PDF p. 15 (printed p. 54), Limitations and future research.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT, accessed through a locally developed Tencent QQ learning system; underlying model/version not stated.
ai_tool.how_used: Learners could address an AI teacher in QQ for continuous personalized questions, answers and guidance before and during class. The system also sent assignment reminders, monitored participation and encouraged critical dialogue. It supplied answers and solutions, so it is not coded as a content-free coach (PDF pp. 5-8, ChatGPT-FLGA and the learning system, Figures 1-6; PDF p. 13, Interview results).

task.description: Design and develop multimedia courseware using Microsoft PowerPoint, including single-choice and flying-centipede animations. The instructional examples invite discussion and creation, but the exact pre- and post-project assessment prompts are not supplied (PDF p. 6, Figures 1-2 and accompanying text; PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure; PDF p. 10, Table 1).
task.duration: The experiment began March 13, 2023: three weeks of introductory knowledge, pre-test and questionnaires in week four, three weeks of assigned learning, and post-test and questionnaires in week eight. Time allowed for producing each assessed project is not stated (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

outcomes.name: Courseware project performance (artifact quality; creativity-scope eligibility uncertain)
outcomes.measure_detail: Two experienced educational-technology instructors scored each pre- and post-project; the student score is their average. The rubric has a maximum of 100 and five dimensions: instruction (fit to teaching needs), science (content errors), technology (materials optimization), artistry (appropriate matching of materials), and operability (interface friendliness). Each dimension has printed levels of 5, 10, 15 and 20 points. Only the composite performance outcome is reported; there are no separate dimension results. Coded usefulness because it assesses artifact quality/appropriateness, but the paper does not explicitly score novelty, originality or overall creativity, and does not supply the exact scored task prompt. ANCOVA controls the corresponding pre-project score (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments and Table 1; PDF p. 11, Experimental results and Table 2).
outcomes.delay: End-of-intervention post-test in week eight following three weeks of assigned learning; no separate retention assessment or elapsed delay in days is stated. Availability of ChatGPT while producing the scored post-project is not stated (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: N = 42, Mean = 88.80, SD = 2.73, Adjusted mean = 89.93, SE = 0.43; Control group: N = 39, Mean = 87.27, SD = 3.41, Adjusted mean = 87.13, SE = 0.45; F = 8.32*, Partial η² = 0.09; table footnote: *p < 0.05. Accompanying prose reports p = 0.00 < 0.05, reproduced as printed. SE values refer to adjusted arm means, not to an arm difference; partial η² is the printed effect measure and no effect size has been computed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 50), Project performance and Table 2; scoring definition in PDF p. 10 (printed p. 49), Table 1.

outcomes.name: Creative thinking tendency (self-report; does not meet the output criterion)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Creative Thinking Tendency Scale from Lai and Hwang (2014): five self-report items, rated from 5 = strongly agree to 1 = strongly disagree; Cronbach’s α = 0.83. Example item: “I like to ask some questions that others do not think of.” This measures reported tendency rather than a score on creative output. ANCOVA controls the pre-questionnaire rating (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments; PDF p. 11, Experimental results; PDF p. 13, Table 8). Retained to document why the paper’s named creativity result cannot establish eligibility.
outcomes.delay: Post-questionnaire administered in week eight at the end of the experiment; this is a self-report response and no creative output is produced (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: N = 42, Mean = 19.19, SD = 3.00, Adjusted mean = 19.07, SE = 0.44; Control group: N = 39, Mean = 17.28, SD = 3.96, Adjusted mean = 17.40, SE = 0.46; F = 6.85*, Partial η² = 0.08; table footnote: *p < 0.05. Accompanying prose reports p = 0.01 < 0.05. SE values refer to adjusted arm means; no effect size has been computed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 13 (printed p. 52), Analysis of creative thinking tendency and Table 8; instrument definition in PDF p. 10 (printed p. 49), Data collection instruments.

company_involvement.description: No company author affiliation or company funding is disclosed. The author is affiliated with Xinjiang Normal University, and the stated funder is the Ministry of Education, China. ChatGPT and Tencent QQ are technologies used in the intervention; their use does not establish company participation in the research.

eligibility.reason: The abstract and Participants section explicitly state random assignment of one of two intact classes to ChatGPT-FLGA, so allocation is coded as a field experiment with class as the randomization unit despite the author’s quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 1 and 9). The study analyzes 81 people, with 42 and 39 in the two groups (PDF p. 9; PDF pp. 11-13, Tables 2-8). Creative thinking tendency is a self-report questionnaire and does not meet the output criterion (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments; PDF p. 13, Table 8). The courseware project composite is genuinely scored on student artifacts and may fit the codebook’s usefulness/quality construct, but its rubric measures teaching fit, correctness, materials optimization/matching and interface friendliness, without explicit creativity or originality scoring; the exact scored task prompt is absent, leaving the creative-task boundary unresolved (PDF pp. 6, 9-11, Figure 2 and Tables 1-2). Core inclusion therefore remains unclear pending that scope judgment. Separately, AI access during production of the scored post-project is unspecified, so with_ai versus after_ai cannot be confirmed from the fact that assessment followed the learning period (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure).

one_line_finding: ChatGPT-FLGA produced higher adjusted courseware-quality scores (89.93 versus 87.13; F = 8.32, p < 0.05) and self-reported creative-thinking tendency (19.07 versus 17.40; F = 6.85, p = 0.01), but the latter is not a creative-output measure and the former’s scope remains uncertain (PDF pp. 11 and 13, Tables 2 and 8).
open_questions: Does the general courseware-quality rubric meet the creative-task/usefulness boundary, and what exactly were students asked to produce in the scored pre- and post-projects? The printed rubric alone does not establish an open-ended creative assessment (PDF pp. 9-11, Experimental procedure and Tables 1-2).

Was ChatGPT available while students produced the scored post-project in week eight, or was that work completed without AI? This is not specified and prevents assignment to with_ai or after_ai (PDF p. 9, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).
notes: All page locators use the PDF page number with the printed journal page in parentheses where useful. The complete markdown conversion was read, including all references; the PDF tables, figures and final pages were checked. Outcome inventory: Table 1 defines the project rubric; Table 2 reports project performance; Table 3 self-efficacy; Table 4 learning attitudes; Table 5 overall learning motivation; Table 6 intrinsic motivation; Table 7 extrinsic motivation; Table 8 creative thinking tendency (PDF pp. 10-13). Figures 1-6 illustrate the learning system and interactions; Figure 7 gives the schedule (PDF pp. 6-9); none reports a scored creativity/diversity contrast. Qualitative interview findings concern learning experiences and perceptions (PDF p. 13). Self-efficacy, attitudes and motivation are excluded from the outcome entries because they are not output scores and answer none of the three atlas questions. Creative-thinking tendency is retained explicitly as an ineligible self-report result; the two recorded outcomes are not two confirmed eligible outcomes. No diversity outcome, separate rubric-dimension comparison, or confirmed unassisted transfer outcome is reported. Preparatory interviews with 10 students and three teachers informed system design (PDF p. 5, Instructional design model), and follow-up interviews involved six students drawn from the experimental/control groups (PDF pp. 9 and 13); these are not additional intervention samples or additional people added to the 81. The design code follows the explicitly stated random assignment of classes, not the author’s quasi-experimental label. There is only one class per condition, and the reported student-level ANCOVA does not describe adjustment for class clustering (PDF pp. 9 and 11). The conventional-learning arm is coded as business as usual because instruction and QQ discussion were shared background provision. Null question/AI-availability fields on the project outcome preserve missing information; mixed would imply documented variation and is not used as an unknown code. The questionnaire AI-availability field is null because there is no scored creative output. Immediate timing denotes the end-of-intervention measurement, not a demonstrated AI-assisted or AI-free production condition. The 89.93 adjusted project mean and the prose p = 0.00 are reproduced exactly as printed, without correction or derived effect sizes. No data/code availability link or preregistration is given.
